newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: PARLIAMENT ADOPTS CONTROVERSIAL LAND LAW.
newsitem.headline: PARLIAMENT ADOPTS CONTROVERSIAL LAND LAW.

text.p: Lithuania's parliament passed a controversial law to restore property to pre-World War Two owners on Thursday, in a vote that strips current occupants of the right to privatise their dwellings.
Critics say the law is divisive, makes tenants second-class citizens and will lead to mass evictions. Fourteen members of parliament abstained from voting.

"The legal status of the owners has been increased and the legal status of occupants is decreased," said Povilas Gylys, member of the opposition Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDDP) and former foreign minister.
"The courts will decide in favour of the owners and we have the potential for tens of thousands of homeless," Gylys said.
The law regulates real estate that was nationalised by the former Soviet Union after it occupied Lithuania in 1940 and how it is to be restored to its former owners.
The law covers the restitution of land, forests, water resevoirs, dwellings and commercial buildings.
It restores land no bigger than 150 hectares including water and forests. The renting of the dwellings is to be handled by the municipalities.
The law's backers say it the establishes continuity of property ownership prior to the 1940 Soviet occupaation.
"It's the restoration of property, of justice and the continuation of the rights of citizens," said Emanuelis Zingeris, a member of the ruling Homeland Union party.
Supporters say the law, which was an iniative by the Conservatives, who dominate parliament and lead the governing coalition, will leave none of the current occupants homeless.

"Not a single owner has the right to move a tenant out," said Arvydas Vidzhiunas, chairman of the Homeland Union parliament faction, saying the only restriction on tenants is on their right to privatise the property.
